title: AQA GCSE Biology · Homeostasis and Response

items.stem: During exercise a person's body temperature rises above its optimum level. Why does the body respond to bring the temperature back down?

options.text: To make the person feel comfortable when hot
To keep optimum conditions for enzyme action
To stop the internal conditions from changing
To let the receptors bring about the cooling

items.why: Homeostasis maintains optimal conditions for enzyme action and all cell functions, so a temperature above the optimum is corrected.

items.stem: The pancreas releases a hormone that lowers a high blood glucose concentration. Which statement about this control system is correct?

options.text: A nervous response restores the optimum level
A chemical response prevents the level changing
A chemical response restores the optimum level
A receptor response restores the optimum level

items.why: Automatic control systems may involve nervous responses or chemical responses; a hormone released by the pancreas is a chemical response, and the optimum blood glucose concentration is restored.

items.stem: A person becomes cold and begins to shiver. Which structure is acting as the effector in this control system?

options.text: the muscles that contract to make the body shiver
the receptors that detect the fall in temperature
the brain that processes information from receptors
the nerves that carry impulses through the body

items.why: Effectors are muscles or glands which bring about responses which restore optimum levels; here muscles contract to produce shivering.

items.stem: Effectors in the human body may be:

options.text: muscles contracting or glands secreting
receptors detecting light and sound levels
skeletal muscles moving bones at a joint
neurones carrying impulses into the brain

items.why: The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

items.stem: A single neurone carries impulses from a receptor in the toe to the spinal cord. Which statement best explains how this structure is adapted to its function?

options.text: It is long, so impulses reach the CNS quickly.
It detects the stimulus and causes the response.
It is part of the central nervous system.
It carries the impulse without using the CNS.

items.why: Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system, so one long cell carries the impulse the whole way to the spinal cord without delay.

items.stem: In a reflex arc, what is the function of the relay neurone?

options.text: It carries the impulse to the conscious brain.
It links the sensory neurone to the motor neurone.
It carries the electrical impulse across the synapse.
It carries the impulse from the skin without the CNS.

items.why: In a reflex arc the sensory neurone passes the impulse across a synapse to a relay neurone in the CNS, which passes it on to the motor neurone that carries the impulse to the effector.

items.stem: Why is a reflex action important when a person touches a very hot object?

options.text: It gives the person time to decide how to act.
It keeps the impulse out of the nervous system.
It is automatic and rapid, so injury is reduced.
It lets the receptor make the response itself.

items.why: Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; the hand is moved away from the stimulus before the conscious part of the brain is involved, which limits the damage done.

items.stem: A patient can no longer coordinate their movements or keep their balance after an injury to the brain. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Damage within the medulla
The cerebellum is damaged
Cerebral cortex is damaged
Damage to the spinal cord

items.why: The cerebellum is the region of the brain responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance, which are the functions the patient has lost.

items.stem: Neuroscientists want to find out which region of a patient's brain controls speech. Which statement explains why this is difficult?

options.text: Damaged brain regions are simple to repair.
MRI scanning shows which cells are working.
Each region of the brain does the same job.
The brain is complex and easily damaged.

items.why: The brain is made of billions of interconnected neurones, and its complexity and delicacy make investigating brain function and treating brain damage and disease very difficult.

items.stem: Which statement correctly relates a structure of the eye to its function?

options.text: The cornea changes shape to focus images.
The iris narrows the pupil in dim lighting.
The ciliary muscles relax for near objects.
The retina contains receptors for light.

items.why: The eye is a sense organ containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour, and these receptors are found in the retina at the back of the eye.

items.stem: A person walks out of bright sunlight into a dark room. What happens in the eye?

options.text: The iris muscles make the pupil narrower.
The ciliary muscles make the lens thicker.
The cornea changes shape to admit light.
The iris muscles make the pupil wider.

items.why: The eye adapts to dim light by the iris muscles widening the pupil, so more light enters the eye and reaches the receptors in the retina.

items.stem: A student looks up from a book and focuses on a tree in the distance. What happens in the eye?

options.text: The ciliary muscles contract and the lens thickens.
The suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens bulges.
The cornea changes shape and the lens stays thin.
The ciliary muscles relax and the lens is pulled thin.

items.why: To focus on a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thin, so it only slightly refracts the light rays.

items.stem: A person is exercising hard and their body temperature rises above normal. What happens in the skin?

options.text: Blood vessels dilate and sweat is produced.
Blood vessels move nearer the skin surface.
Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
The skin cools the body without the brain.

items.why: If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands; both mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.

items.stem: A person waits at a bus stop in cold weather and their body temperature begins to fall. How does the body raise it again?

options.text: Blood vessels dilate and shivering begins.
Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
Narrowing blood vessels cause the shivering.
The skin warms the blood without using the brain.

items.why: If the body temperature is too low, blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction) and sweating stops, reducing energy transfer from the skin, while skeletal muscles contract (shiver), releasing energy that warms the body.

items.stem: A table shows one student's mean reaction time in three trials: trial 1, 0.28 s; trial 2, 0.24 s; trial 3, 0.21 s. What do these data show?

options.text: The reaction time fell across the trials.
The reaction time rose across the trials.
The student reacted more slowly each time.
The results apply to other students too.

items.why: Reading the values in order from the table shows a decrease from 0.28 s to 0.21 s, which is the pattern the data support.

items.stem: Four students have mean reaction times of 0.15 s, 0.22 s, 0.28 s and 0.31 s. These values are drawn as a bar chart. Which statement about the chart is correct?

options.text: The tallest bar is the fastest time.
The shortest bar is the slowest time.
The tallest bar is the 0.31 s time.
Each bar stands for the whole group.

items.why: Translating the numbers into graphical form, bar height is proportional to reaction time, so the largest value, 0.31 s, gives the tallest bar.

items.stem: A ray diagram shows light from a distant object coming to a focus in front of the retina. Which defect is shown, and how is it corrected?

options.text: Myopia, corrected with a convex lens.
Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens.
Myopia, corrected with a concave lens.
Hyperopia, corrected with a concave lens.

items.why: Rays focusing in front of the retina show myopia (short sightedness); a concave spectacle lens spreads the rays out so that they do focus on the retina.

items.stem: A gland of the endocrine system secretes a hormone. How does that hormone reach the organ where it produces an effect, and how do its effects compare with those of the nervous system?

options.text: carried along nerves; effects are slower but last longer
carried in the blood; effects are faster but end much sooner
carried along nerves; effects are faster but end sooner
carried in the blood; effects are slower but last longer

items.why: Glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream and the blood carries the hormone to a target organ; compared to the nervous system the effects are slower but act for longer.

items.stem: Why is the pituitary gland described as a 'master gland'?

options.text: its hormones make other glands release hormones
its hormones produce all the body effects directly
its hormones travel to the glands along nerves
its hormones act on every organ in the body

items.why: The pituitary gland secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions, and these act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released.

items.stem: What causes Type 1 diabetes?

options.text: the body cells no longer respond to insulin
the pancreas releases insulin when glucose is low
the pancreas fails to produce enough insulin
the pancreas is affected by a person's diet

items.why: Type 1 diabetes is a disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, and it is characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels.

items.stem: Which statement about the loss of water and other substances from the body is correct?

options.text: water lost in sweat is controlled by hormones
sweat contains water but no ions or urea
water lost from the lungs is not controlled
water lost from the skin is closely controlled

items.why: Water leaves the body via the lungs during exhalation, and there is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the lungs or skin.

items.stem: What is the role of follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) in the menstrual cycle?

options.text: it causes a mature egg to be released
it keeps the lining of the uterus in place
it causes an egg to mature in the ovary
it is released from the ovary at puberty

items.why: Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.

items.stem: How do oral contraceptives that contain hormones prevent pregnancy?

options.text: they inhibit FSH production so no eggs mature
they kill or disable sperm before fertilisation
they stop an embryo implanting in the uterus
they form a barrier that stops sperm reaching eggs

items.why: Oral contraceptives contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature.

items.stem: Which statement about IVF treatment is correct?

options.text: eggs are fertilised by sperm in the laboratory
eggs are fertilised by the sperm inside the mother
most IVF treatments result in a successful birth
multiple births from IVF carry very little risk

items.why: In IVF the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory; the embryos are inserted into the uterus as tiny balls of cells.

items.stem: Which statement about the main reproductive hormones is correct?

options.text: oestrogen is produced by the pituitary gland
testosterone is produced by the testes
oestrogen is produced by the thyroid gland
testosterone is produced by the pituitary

items.why: Testosterone is the main male reproductive hormone produced by the testes, and it stimulates sperm production.

items.stem: A student labels endocrine glands on a diagram of the human body. Which label has been placed in the correct position?

options.text: the adrenal gland labelled inside the brain
the thyroid gland labelled in the lower neck
the pituitary gland labelled below the stomach
the pancreas labelled at the base of the brain

items.why: The thyroid is found in the neck, and students should be able to identify its position on a diagram of the human body.

items.stem: After a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person who does not have diabetes rises above the normal level. What happens next?

options.text: insulin is released and glycogen forms in the blood
insulin is released and so glucose leaves the cells
insulin is released but the cells fail to respond
insulin is released and glucose enters the cells

items.why: If the blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas produces the hormone insulin that causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.

items.stem: A person's blood glucose concentration is too high. What happens to the excess glucose?

options.text: it is changed into glycogen in the blood
it is released from the cells into the blood
it is changed into glycogen in the pancreas
it moves into cells and is stored as glycogen

items.why: Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells, and in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.

items.stem: The body fluids around a person's cells become too dilute. What is the effect on the cells?

options.text: they gain water by osmosis and work as normal
they gain water by osmosis and work less well
they lose water by osmosis and stop working well
they lose water by osmosis and work as normal

items.why: Water moves into the cells by osmosis from the more dilute body fluids, and if body cells gain too much water by osmosis they do not function efficiently.

items.stem: How do the kidneys produce urine and help to maintain the water balance of the body?

options.text: only waste substances are filtered out of the blood
glucose and all useful ions are lost in the urine
urea is reabsorbed and glucose is lost in the urine
the blood is filtered and useful substances reabsorbed

items.why: The kidneys produce urine by filtration of the blood and selective reabsorption of useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water, and excess water, ions and urea are removed in the urine.

items.stem: On a hot day a person sweats a great deal and drinks very little, so the blood becomes too concentrated. What is the effect of ADH on the kidney tubules?

options.text: they become less permeable, so water is reabsorbed
they become more permeable, so more urine is produced
they become more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed
they become less permeable, so more sweat is produced

items.why: ADH is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated and acts on the kidney tubules, making them more permeable so that more water is reabsorbed back into the blood.

items.stem: Which statement describes a basic principle of kidney dialysis?

options.text: glucose passes from the blood into the dialysis fluid
urea passes from the blood into the dialysis fluid
useful ions pass from the blood into the fluid
water and ions pass from the blood into the fluid

items.why: Dialysis treats kidney failure by allowing urea to pass out of the blood into a dialysis fluid that contains no urea, while useful substances are not lost.

items.stem: A woman wants a method of contraception that does not use hormones. Which method and reason are correct?

options.text: a condom, which releases a hormone slowly
a diaphragm, which stops sperm reaching eggs
the pill, which kills sperm before they arrive
an implant, which stops sperm reaching an egg

items.why: Barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms prevent the sperm reaching an egg, so they control fertility without using hormones.

items.stem: A woman does not release eggs because her level of FSH is too low. Which treatment could allow her to become pregnant in the normal way?

options.text: a fertility drug that contains FSH and LH
a fertility drug that contains progesterone
IVF, in which eggs are fertilised in her body
a fertility drug that contains only LH

items.why: Giving FSH and LH in a 'fertility drug' to a woman stimulates the maturation and release of eggs, and she may then become pregnant in the normal way.

items.stem: A student is suddenly frightened by a loud noise. Which gland releases adrenaline, and what effect does it have?

options.text: the adrenal gland; it raises the heart rate
the pituitary gland; it raises the heart rate
the thyroid gland; it reduces the heart rate
the pituitary gland; it lowers the heart rate

items.why: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles.

items.stem: The concentration of thyroxine in the blood of a person rises above the normal level. What happens next?

options.text: more thyroxine is released and the level rises
the metabolic rate falls and the level stays high
the metabolic rate falls and more thyroxine forms
thyroxine release is inhibited and the level falls

items.why: Thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback, so a level above normal inhibits the release of thyroxine until the level returns to normal.

items.stem: A person with Type 2 diabetes has a normal concentration of insulin in the blood but a high blood glucose concentration. Why?

options.text: their pancreas has completely stopped making insulin
their insulin cannot act on glucose in the blood
their body cells no longer respond to insulin
their insulin is released when blood glucose is low

items.why: In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells even though insulin is present.

items.stem: A graph shows blood glucose concentration for two hours after a glucose drink. For a person without diabetes the concentration rises to a peak and then returns to its starting level. For a person with untreated Type 1 diabetes it rises higher and stays high. What does the graph show about the person with Type 1 diabetes?

options.text: not enough insulin is produced to lower glucose
their body cells have stopped responding to insulin
their insulin cannot change glucose to glycogen
their insulin is produced when glucose is low

items.why: The concentration stays high because the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells and the level is not brought back down.

items.stem: Several hours after a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person falls below the normal level. Which change restores it?

options.text: insulin is released and stored glycogen changes to glucose
glucagon is released and glucose changes to glycogen
glucagon is released and glycogen changes to glucose
insulin is released and glucose changes to glycogen

items.why: If the blood glucose concentration is too low, the pancreas produces glucagon, which causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.

items.stem: A table gives the concentration of two substances in the blood entering a kidney and in the urine leaving it, in grams per dm3. Glucose: 1.0 in the blood and 0.0 in the urine. Urea: 0.3 in the blood and 20.0 in the urine. What do these figures show?

options.text: glucose is not filtered, so none reaches the urine
glucose is reabsorbed, so it is absent from urine
glucose is removed with the urea and lost from blood
urea and glucose are both reabsorbed by the kidney

items.why: The blood is filtered and glucose is a useful substance that is selectively reabsorbed, so its concentration in the urine falls to zero while urea becomes concentrated.

items.stem: Which interaction between hormones helps to control the menstrual cycle?

options.text: LH inhibits FSH and causes an egg to mature
FSH inhibits oestrogen and maintains the lining
progesterone stimulates FSH and LH release
oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH release

items.why: Oestrogen produced in the ovary inhibits the production of FSH and stimulates the release of LH, which then stimulates the release of the egg.

items.stem: A graph of hormone levels during the menstrual cycle shows the level of LH rising to a sharp peak on day 14. What is happening on day 14?

options.text: an egg is starting to mature in the ovary
an egg is being released from the ovary
the lining of the uterus is being maintained
the lining of the uterus is breaking down

items.why: Luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg, so a sharp peak in LH on day 14 indicates ovulation.

items.stem: Which effect of a plant hormone is described correctly?

options.text: Gibberellins are important in initiating seed germination.
Ethene is important in initiating germination of seeds.
Gibberellins are important in maintaining seed dormancy.
Ethene is important in preventing the ripening of fruits.

items.why: This is the stated effect of gibberellins: they are important in initiating seed germination.

items.stem: A young shoot is lit from one side only and bends towards the light. Which explains this?

options.text: Auxin gathers on the lit side, which grows faster.
Auxin gathers on the shaded side, which grows less.
Auxin gathers on the shaded side, which grows faster.
Auxin gathers on the lit side, which then grows slower.

items.why: Unequal distribution of auxin gives more auxin on the shaded side of the shoot, which produces a faster growth rate on that side, so the shoot bends towards the light (phototropism).

items.stem: A seedling is laid on its side in the dark. Which describes the response of its root?

options.text: Auxin gathers on the lower side, which grows more quickly.
Auxin collects on the upper side, which grows slower.
Auxin gathers on the lower side, which grows slower.
Auxin gathers on the upper side, which then grows faster.

items.why: Unequal distribution of auxin gives more auxin on the lower side of the root, where it causes a slower growth rate, so the root bends downwards (gravitropism or geotropism).

items.stem: A farmer sprays a field of cereal plants with a weed killer containing auxins. What is the result?

options.text: The weeds and the cereal crop are both killed off.
The weeds and the cereal crop both grow faster now.
The cereal dies and the weeds keep on growing.
The weeds die and the cereal crop keeps growing.

items.why: Auxins are used as weed killers in agriculture: the hormone upsets the growth of the weeds so that they die, while the cereal crop is unaffected.

items.stem: Bananas are picked unripe and kept cool while they are shipped. Ethene is used on them when they arrive. Why?

options.text: To stop the fruit from ripening while it is stored.
To start the fruit ripening at the end of storage.
To keep the fruit firm until it is in the shops.
To make the seeds inside the fruit start growing.

items.why: Ethene controls the ripening of fruits and is used in the food industry to control ripening during storage and transport, so the fruit ripens when it is wanted.

items.stem: A grower treats a fruit crop with gibberellins. Which result would be expected?

options.text: The fruits ripen early, before reaching full size.
The seeds inside the fruits are kept in dormancy.
The treated plants are killed off by the spray.
The fruits grow larger than untreated fruits.

items.why: Gibberellins can be used to increase fruit size, which is one of the ways plant growth hormones are used in agriculture and horticulture.
